rv.q: Close's return to the role that made her a Broadway legend is nothing short of triumphant, a master class in musical theater acting that reminds you why she owned this part in the first place.
The audacity of this performance is matched by its veracity.
Close is divine in these early glimpses of Norma, obviously batty, but clinging to her dreams (and her sanity), and sustained by Max’s ministrations.
Close's performance is a master class in controlled hysteria, a study in how an actress can make a character's delusions feel both pathetic and magnificent.
Close's return that is this revival's reason for being, and the rapturous audience reaction makes it clear she owns the role.
Like the merchandise, the show is a limited edition selling paste and glitter as treasures.
Ms. Close's performance is a tour de force of theatrical artifice, but the production around her feels oddly cramped and underpowered
Her masterful portrayal also delivers the one thing poor nutty Norma most craves: An adoring, utterly captivated audience, and applause that echoes long after the curtain falls.
Glenn Close's return to Norma Desmond is a master class in musical theater performance, even if the production around her doesn't quite match her magnificence.
The moment is as good as musical-theater gets.

Director Lonny Price and his lead actress seem determined to force you out of the moment, overloading the production with so many "Major Theatrical Event" moments and signposts that it all starts to sag beneath the weight of its own self-importance.
And as Close portrays her, she is a universal character, embittered by her faded glory to the point of being delusional.

Of all the big names attached to this production, the most important is Billy Wilder. The 1950 film which he co-wrote and directed is so chock full of bullet-proof source material – weird characters, classic lines, unforgettable freeze frames – it is impossible not to be entertained by any decent adaptation.
